claim: Tuberculosis is a heterogeneous disease in humans with individuals exhibiting a wide range of susceptibility.
source: Tuberculosis is a heterogeneous disease in humans with individuals exhibiting a wide range of susceptibility.
evidence: This is a general statement about TB disease heterogeneity that is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Standard laboratory mouse lines do not capture the heterogeneity of tuberculosis disease seen in humans.
source: This heterogeneity is not captured by standard laboratory mouse lines.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of standard mouse models that is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Wild-derived mice have heterogeneous immune responses to Mtb infection.
source: Wild-derived mice have heterogeneous immune responses to infection that result in differential ability to control disease at early time points.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing variability in immune responses across different wild-derived mouse lines.

claim: Enhanced control of Mtb infection is associated with increased numbers of CD4 T cells, CD8 T cells, and B cells.
source: Correlation analysis with multiple parameters including sex, weight, and cellular immune responses in the lungs revealed that enhanced control of infection is associated with increased numbers of CD4 T cells, CD8 T cells, and B cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis data presented in Figure 2F-I showing relationships between these cell types and bacterial burden.

claim: Strong correlations between IFN-γ production and control of infection were not observed in wild-derived mice.
source: Surprisingly, we did not observe strong correlations between IFN-γ production and control of infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B showing lack of correlation between IFN-γ+ CD4 T cells and CFU.

claim: A mouse line that harbors high neutrophil numbers yet controls infection was identified.
source: Although in most lines high neutrophils were associated with susceptibility, we identified a mouse line that harbors high neutrophil numbers yet controls infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing MANB mice have high neutrophils but control infection (Figure 4A-C).

claim: A novel neutrophil signature associated with failure to control infection was identified using single-cell RNA sequencing.
source: Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we identified a novel neutrophil signature associated with failure to control infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data presented in Figures 4K-M and Figure 5 showing distinct transcriptional profiles of MANC neutrophils.

claim: The majority of Mtb-infected individuals never develop active disease and are able to control infection for their lifetimes.
source: Whereas the majority of infected individuals never develop active disease and are able to control infection for their lifetimes, some individuals are highly susceptible to infection and develop active tuberculosis (TB).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TB disease outcomes in humans.

claim: Patients with active TB disease show heterogeneity in disease progression.
source: Patients with active disease show heterogeneity in disease progression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TB disease variability.

claim: The timing of disease onset after initial Mtb infection varies from individual to individual.
source: Additionally, the timing of disease onset after initial infection and disease outcome varies from individual to individual (Cadena et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: TB is a complex genetic disease.
source: This heterogeneity in human responses suggests that TB is a complex genetic disease.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed heterogeneity in human responses to TB.

claim: GWAS studies have identified IFNG, IFNGR1, IL12B, and IL12RB1 as genetic factors that underlie variability of responses to Mtb in humans.
source: Indeed, GWAS studies have identified a small number of genetic factors that underlie the variability of responses to Mtb in humans including interferon-γ (IFNG), interferon-γ receptor (IFNGR1), interleukin-12 subunit p40 (IL12B), and interleukin-12 receptor b-1 chain (IL12RB1) (Qu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published GWAS studies.

claim: New vaccine candidates that elicit IFN-γ producing T cells in human volunteers do not elicit complete protection from Mtb infection.
source: Despite the clear importance of IFN-γ for control of mycobacterial infection, new vaccine candidates that elicit IFN-γ producing T cells in human volunteers do not elicit complete protection from infection, suggesting that additional protective mechanisms that have yet to be identified may be essential (Tameris et al., 2013; Tait et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published vaccine studies.

claim: Type I IFN and neutrophils have been associated with active TB disease in patients.
source: Similarly, several immune signatures have been associated with active disease in TB patients, including type I IFN and neutrophils (Donovan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The mouse model of TB infection captures much of what is known about human immune responses to Mtb, including the importance of CD4 T cells and IFN-γ for immune control of infection.
source: Importantly, the mouse model captures much of what is known about human immune responses to Mtb, including the importance of CD4 T cells and IFN-γ for immune control of infection (Green et al., 2013; Caruso et al., 1999; Flynn et al., 1993; Scanga et al., 2000; Cooper et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Current mouse models fail to recapitulate spontaneous resolution of Mtb infection.
source: However, current mouse models fail to recapitulate several aspects of Mtb infection, including spontaneous resolution of infection as well as the widely varying susceptibility and patterns of disease seen in humans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about limitations of current mouse models.

claim: Most commonly used mouse lines exhibit similar infection dynamics and characteristics during Mtb infection.
source: Although there are minor differences in susceptibility to infection, most commonly used mouse lines all exhibit similar infection dynamics and characteristics.
evidence: This is established knowledge about standard laboratory mouse lines.

claim: The Sst1 locus regulates type I IFN signaling through the gene Sp140.
source: An example is the characterization of the Sst1 locus, which regulates type I IFN signaling through the gene Sp140, a repressor of type I IFN (Ji et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2005; Kramnik et al., 2000; Kramnik et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Sst1 susceptible mice have a loss of function mutation of Sp140.
source: Excessive production of type I IFN in Sst1 susceptible (Sst1s) mice, which have a loss of function mutation of Sp140, elicits increased IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL1-Ra) expression which competes with IL-1 for binding to the IL-1R.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature about the Sst1 locus.

claim: IL-1 is crucial for control of Mtb infection.
source: IL-1 is crucial for control of infection and the functional deficiency in IL-1 signaling in Sst1s mice results in increased susceptibility to Mtb (Ji et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Collaborative Cross model was founded by crossing five common laboratory lines and three wild-derived lines.
source: The Collaborative Cross (CC) model was founded by crossing five common laboratory lines and three wild-derived lines (Churchill et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Diversity Outbred mice are currently the most diverse mouse resource available.
source: This is currently the most diverse mouse resource available (Svenson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Infection of Diversity Outbred mice with Mtb revealed correlations between disease pathology and neutrophil influx.
source: Infection of the DO cohort with Mtb revealed correlations between disease pathology and neutrophil influx, recapitulating features seen in human lung infections, in addition to identifying new inflammatory biomarkers that correlate with active human disease (Niazi et al., 2015; Koyuncu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The susceptibility of the CC042 line is associated with the loss of Itgal expression.
source: For example, the susceptibility of the CC042 line is associated with the loss of Itgal expression, an integrin required for T cell trafficking to the lung, resulting in decreased T cell trafficking and IFN-γ production in the lungs of infected animals (Smith et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A new collection of 19 inbred lines was derived from wild mice collected across different geographic regions.
source: To increase the genetic diversity of house mice available for the analysis of complex phenotypes, researchers recently created a set of 19 new inbred lines derived from wild mice collected across different geographic regions (Phifer-Rixey et al., 2018; Moeller et al., 2018; Suzuki et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The new wild-derived inbred lines are all from the Mus musculus domesticus subspecies of house mouse.
source: Unlike CC and DO mice, these new lines are all from the Mus musculus domesticus subspecies of house mouse.
evidence: This is a statement about the genetic composition of the mouse lines used in the study.

claim: Each wild-derived line has been inbred through sib-sib mating for at least 10 generations.
source: Each line has been inbred through sib–sib mating for at least 10 generations, providing the benefit of the genetic reproducibility of laboratory-derived lines.
evidence: This is a statement about the breeding history of the mouse lines.

claim: This is the first report of the use of this collection of mice for infectious disease or immunology-related phenotypes.
source: This is the first report of the use of this collection of mice for infectious disease or immunology-related phenotypes.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: The cohort of wild-derived mice was established using outbred mice originally collected from five different localities across the Americas.
source: The cohort of wild-derived mice used in this study was established using outbred mice originally collected from five different localities across the Americas: Edmonton (EDM), Alberta, Canada; Saratoga Springs (SAR), New York, United States of America; Gainesville (GAI), Florida, United States of America; Tucson (TUC), Arizona, United States of America; and Manaus (MAN), Amazonas, Brazil (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the text description and Figure 1A showing the collection sites.

claim: Wild-derived mice exhibit phenotypic differences including body weight, body length, body mass index, and glucose and lipid metabolism.
source: These mice exhibit a variety of phenotypic differences, including body weight, body length, body mass index (BMI), and glucose and lipid metabolism (Phifer-Rixey et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Separate lines of mice collected from a single location are in general more closely related genetically than mice collected from different locales.
source: Although there is within-group heterogeneity, separate lines of mice collected from a single location are in general more closely related genetically than mice collected from different locales (Ferris et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The median bacterial burden varied over 100-fold between mice from different locales at 21 days post-infection.
source: The median bacterial burden varied over 100-fold between mice from different locales (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B showing CFU measurements.

claim: Individual mouse lines that originated from the same locale demonstrated a wide variation in susceptibility to Mtb.
source: Surprisingly, individual mouse lines that originated from the same locale demonstrated a wide variation in susceptibility, suggesting that genetic heterogeneity within the closely related lines can influence the outcome of infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 1C and 1D showing variation within locales.

claim: Bacterial burdens in the lungs of MANC mice are significantly higher compared to MANA, MANB, and MANE lines.
source: Bacterial burdens in the lungs of mice from the MANC line are significantly higher compared to the closely related MANA, MANB, and MANE lines which are approximately as resistant as the standard B6 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1C showing CFU measurements.

claim: SARA and SARC mice are at least as resistant to Mtb infection as the standard B6.
source: Whereas SARA and SARC mice are at least as resistant to infection as the standard B6, SARB lines harbor significantly more bacteria in the lungs at 3 weeks post-infection (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1D showing CFU measurements.

claim: SARB mice harbor significantly more bacteria in the lungs at 3 weeks post-infection compared to B6.
source: Whereas SARA and SARC mice are at least as resistant to infection as the standard B6, SARB lines harbor significantly more bacteria in the lungs at 3 weeks post-infection (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1D showing CFU measurements.

claim: A low BMI has been shown to be a risk factor for TB in humans.
source: A low BMI has been shown to be a risk factor for TB in humans (Lönnroth et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: No correlation was found between body weight and TB control in well-nourished wild-derived mice.
source: However, we did not find a correlation between body weight and TB control in these well-nourished mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: No differences in bacterial burden at 21 days post-infection were observed between male and female wild-derived mice.
source: We also observed no differences in bacterial burden at 21 days post-infection between male and female mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F comparing sexes.

claim: Demonstrated differences in the ability of male and female mice to control Mtb infection emerged only at late time points ~200 days after infection.
source: This is not surprising, as demonstrated differences in the ability of male and female mice to control infection emerged only at late time points ~200 days after infection (Dibbern et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Variability was observed in the relative proportions of macrophages, neutrophils, CD4 T cells, CD8 T cells, and B cells when comparing individual wild-derived mouse lines.
source: We observed variability in the relative proportions of macrophages, neutrophils, CD4 T cells, CD8 T cells, and B cells when comparing individual lines (Figure 2A–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figures 2A-E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The most striking differences observed in wild-derived mice were in CD11b+Ly6G+ neutrophils.
source: The most striking differences observed were in CD11b+Ly6G+ neutrophils, both when comparing individual lines isolated from a single geographic site and when comparing mice originally derived from different locales (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figures 2A-E.

claim: Significant correlations were found between the proportion of CD3+, CD4+, CD8+, and B220+ cells with control of Mtb infection.
source: We found significant correlations between the proportion of CD3+, CD4+, CD8+, and B220+ cells with control of infection, with larger proportions of these cells corresponding to lower CFU in the lung (Figure 2F–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis data presented in Figures 2F-I.

claim: The proportion of neutrophils in the lung could explain approximately 60% of the variation in bacterial burden in wild-derived mice.
source: In contrast, we found that the proportion of neutrophils in the lung could explain approximately 60% of the variation seen in the wild-derived mice, with higher neutrophil burden associated with higher CFU in the lungs (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis data presented in Figure 2J.

claim: Higher neutrophil burden is associated with higher CFU in the lungs of wild-derived mice.
source: In contrast, we found that the proportion of neutrophils in the lung could explain approximately 60% of the variation seen in the wild-derived mice, with higher neutrophil burden associated with higher CFU in the lungs (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis data presented in Figure 2J.

claim: Excessive infiltration of neutrophils promotes lung pathology and susceptibility to Mtb infection in susceptible mice on the B6 background.
source: This is consistent with numerous studies of susceptible mice on the B6 background that have pointed to a role for excessive infiltration of neutrophils in promoting lung pathology and susceptibility to Mtb infection (Kimmey et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2017; Nair et al., 2018; Dorhoi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: B6 mice exhibit a high proportion of IFN-γ producing CD4 T cells and lower bacterial burden in the lungs compared to several wild mice lines.
source: As expected, B6 mice exhibit a high proportion of IFN-γ producing CD4 T cells and lower bacterial burden in the lungs compared to several wild mice lines (Figure 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and CFU data presented in Figure 2K.

claim: The SARA line controls bacterial CFU in the lungs in the presence of very few IFN-γ producing CD4 T cells.
source: The SARA line controls bacterial CFU in the lungs in the presence of very few IFN-γ producing CD4 T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: No correlations were found between bacterial burden and the proportion of IFN-γ producing CD8 T cells or CD11b+ cells.
source: No correlations were found between bacterial burden and the proportion of IFN-γ producing CD8 T cells or CD11b+ cells (Figure 2L, M).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis data presented in Figures 2L and 2M.

claim: Macrophages from all tested Manaus lines allow the growth of Mtb in the absence of exogenous cytokine stimulation.
source: Macrophages from all the tested lines, including B6, allow the growth of Mtb in the absence of exogenous cytokine stimulation (Figure 3A), with none of the lines exhibiting a loss of control relative to B6.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro infection data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: A slight decrease in bacterial replication was observed in MANB, MANC, and MANE macrophages relative to B6.
source: Indeed, we observed a slight decrease in bacterial replication in MANB, MANC, and MANE relative to B6 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro infection data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: All Manaus macrophages responded similarly to IFN-γ stimulation, producing significantly more nitric oxide upon infection than B6.
source: Additionally, all macrophages responded similarly to IFN-γ stimulation, producing significantly more nitric oxide (NO) upon infection than is observed with B6 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Griess assay data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: All MAN lines controlled Mtb infection as well or better than B6 in IFN-γ-activated macrophages.
source: Similarly, we did not observe any defects in IFN-γ-based control of infection at the macrophage level as all MAN lines controlled infection as well or better than the standard B6 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro infection data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Differences in cell intrinsic control of infection that are evident ex vivo do not obviously play a role in the susceptibility of the MANC line to Mtb infection.
source: Thus, differences in cell intrinsic control of infection that are evident ex vivo do not obviously play a role in the susceptibility of the MANC line to Mtb infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vitro macrophage data showing no defects in MANC macrophages.

claim: Type I IFN is a major driver of susceptibility in mice and possibly humans.
source: Type I IFN is known to be a major driver of susceptibility in mice, and possibly humans (Ji et al., 2019; Dorhoi et al., 2014; Desvignes et al., 2012; Antonelli et al., 2010; Berry et al., 2010; Zak et al., 2016; Singhania et al., 2018; Scriba et al., 2017; Llibre et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Macrophages from three MAN lines (MANC, MANB, and MANE) produced significantly more type I IFN than B6 or MANA.
source: We found that macrophages isolated from three MAN lines (MANC, MANB, and MANE) produced significantly more type I IFN than B6 or MANA (Figure 3D); however, these findings did not correlate with the ability to control infection in vivo (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by type I IFN bioactivity assay data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Type I IFN production by macrophages from MAN lines did not correlate with the ability to control infection in vivo.
source: We found that macrophages isolated from three MAN lines (MANC, MANB, and MANE) produced significantly more type I IFN than B6 or MANA (Figure 3D); however, these findings did not correlate with the ability to control infection in vivo (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of type I IFN data (Figure 3D) with in vivo CFU data (Figure 1C).

claim: In vitro production of IL-1 by infected macrophages from Manaus lines was comparable to B6.
source: We also measured IL-1 bioactivity in the supernatants of infected macrophages using the HEK-Blue IL-1R cell line and found that in vitro production of IL-1 was comparable to other Manaus genotypes and to B6.
evidence: This claim is supported by IL-1 bioactivity assay data (Figure 3E implied).

claim: None of the Manaus lines appear to have major macrophage intrinsic defects that would explain the observed differences in control of infection in vivo.
source: Taken together, unlike the majority of susceptible mouse lines, none of the Manaus lines appear to have major macrophage intrinsic defects observable that would explain the observed differences in control of infection in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vitro macrophage characterization data.

claim: Neutrophils are generally associated with active disease and pathogenesis in human TB.
source: In human TB, neutrophils are generally associated with active disease and pathogenesis (Gopal et al., 2013; Eum et al., 2010; Lowe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The vast majority of mouse lines with excessive accumulation of neutrophils in the lung have high bacterial burdens and are susceptible to Mtb infection.
source: The vast majority of mouse lines with excessive accumulation of neutrophils in the lung have high bacterial burdens in the lung and are susceptible to infection (Niazi et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2017; Nandi and Behar, 2011; Eruslanov et al., 2005; Lyadova et al., 2010; Marzo et al., 2014; Keller et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The majority of Manaus lines show high neutrophilic influx to the lungs compared to B6 mice, despite variability in bacterial burden.
source: Interestingly, the majority of the Manaus lines show high neutrophilic influx to the lungs compared to B6 mice, despite the strong variability in bacterial burden (Figures 1C and 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 1C and 2A.

claim: The proportion of neutrophils in the lung is a clear predictor of susceptibility to Mtb infection across all wild-derived lines examined (r = 0.6803).
source: In general, the proportion of neutrophils in the lung is a clear predictor of susceptibility to infection across all lines examined (Figure 2J, r = 0.6803).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis data presented in Figure 2J.

claim: A significantly decreased correlation was found between the proportion of neutrophils in the lungs and total CFU in mice from Manaus.
source: However, when examining mice from Manaus, we found a significantly decreased correlation in the proportion of neutrophils in the lungs and the total CFU, in line with our initial observation that these mice tend to have a higher proportion of neutrophils in the lungs than B6 despite variability in CFU (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Mice from Manaus may have phenotypic heterogeneity in neutrophil populations that results in diminished correlation between neutrophils and susceptibility to infection.
source: These data suggest that mice from Manaus may have phenotypic heterogeneity in neutrophil populations that results in diminished correlation between neutrophils and susceptibility to infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decreased correlation between neutrophils and CFU in Manaus mice.

claim: Manaus mice controlled Mtb infection as well as B6 mice at 25 days post-infection, with the exception of the MANC line.
source: Mice from Manaus controlled infection with Mtb as well as B6 mice, as measured by CFU in the lungs at 25 days post-infection, with the exception of the MANC line (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by CFU data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: All Manaus mice have a higher proportion of neutrophils in the lungs compared to B6.
source: All Manaus mice have a higher proportion of neutrophils in the lungs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: MANB and MANC had elevated, roughly equivalent, absolute numbers of neutrophils in the lungs despite very different bacterial burdens.
source: In addition, when comparing the absolute number of neutrophils in the lungs of infected mice, MANB and MANC had elevated, roughly equivalent, absolute numbers of neutrophils in the lungs (Figure 4C), despite very different bacterial burdens (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: Antibody depletion of neutrophils resulted in a dramatic drop of ~40-fold in CFU in the lungs of MANC mice.
source: Antibody depletion resulted in a dramatic drop of ~40-fold in CFU in the lungs of MANC mice (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by neutrophil depletion experiment data presented in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: Depleting neutrophils from B6 or MANB mice had a more modest effect on CFU burden of two- to threefold.
source: In contrast, depleting neutrophils from B6 or MANB mice had a more modest effect on CFU burden of two- to threefold (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by neutrophil depletion experiment data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: In MANC mice, neutrophils are an important driver of susceptibility to Mtb.
source: Thus, in MANC mice, neutrophils are an important driver of susceptibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on the neutrophil depletion experiment showing dramatic reduction in CFU when neutrophils are depleted.

claim: Neutrophils in MANC lesions appeared to form large aggregates of cells.
source: Whereas neutrophils appeared as discrete cells within lesions of MANB mice (Figure 4G), neutrophils in MANC lesions appeared to form large aggregates of cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data presented in Figures 4G and 4H.

claim: There was twice the amount of neutrophil staining per area in MANC lesions relative to MANB.
source: In addition, there was twice the amount of neutrophil staining per area in MANC lesions relative to MANB (Figure 4I) and far fewer CD4 T cells within MANC lesions than within MANB lesions (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 4I.

claim: There were far fewer CD4 T cells within MANC lesions than within MANB lesions.
source: In addition, there was twice the amount of neutrophil staining per area in MANC lesions relative to MANB (Figure 4I) and far fewer CD4 T cells within MANC lesions than within MANB lesions (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 4J.

claim: The cell type composition was relatively similar across B6, MANA, MANB, and MANC genotypes based on scRNAseq analysis.
source: Overall, transcriptional profiles indicated that the cell type composition was relatively similar across genotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq analysis of lung immune cells.

claim: An increase in cells identified as neutrophils was observed in both MANB and MANC mice relative to other genotypes based on scRNAseq.
source: The exception was an increase in cells identified as neutrophils (Ly6g+, S100a8+) in both MANB and MANC mice relative to the other genotypes, consistent with our flow cytometry data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D-G).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D-G.

claim: Neutrophils clustered into 2 major populations and at least 10 well-defined subpopulations based on scRNAseq analysis.
source: Neutrophils clustered into 2 major populations (Figure 4K) and at least 10 well-defined subpopulations (Figure 4L).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq clustering analysis presented in Figures 4K and 4L.

claim: B6, MANA, and MANB neutrophils clustered together while MANC neutrophils remained quite distinct.
source: B6, MANA, and MANB neutrophils clustered together while MANC neutrophils remained quite distinct.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq clustering analysis presented in Figure 4K.

claim: MANC neutrophils exhibited the most within-genotype heterogeneity in neutrophil subsets.
source: MANC clustered separately from neutrophils of any of the other genotypes and exhibited the most within-genotype heterogeneity in neutrophil subsets (Figure 4K, L).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq clustering analysis presented in Figures 4K and 4L.

claim: Neutrophils from MANC mice were enriched for GO biological processes indicative of neutrophil activation.
source: Aggregated together, neutrophils from MANC mice were enriched for GO biological processes indicative of neutrophil activation, including positive regulation of neutrophil activation, neutrophil degranulation, superoxide generation, and glycolysis (Figure 4M).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis data presented in Figure 4M.

claim: GO processes downregulated in MANC neutrophils relative to B6 included antigen processing, prostaglandin biosynthesis, and NOD signaling.
source: GO processes downregulated in MANC neutrophils relative to B6 included antigen processing, prostaglandin biosynthesis, and NOD signaling (Figure 4M).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis data presented in Figure 4M.

claim: Neutrophils from MANC mice are more activated and more likely to be engaging in processes that result in destruction of host tissue.
source: These data suggest that neutrophils from MANC mice are more activated and more likely to be engaging in processes that result in destruction of host tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GO enrichment analysis showing enrichment for neutrophil activation processes.

claim: MANC neutrophils scored higher across neutrophil activation, NADPH oxidase, and secretory vesicles parameters than any other genotype tested, including Sp140–/–.
source: In all cases, we found that MANC neutrophils scored higher across the parameters than any other genotype tested, including Sp140–/– (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by neutrophil signature scoring data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neutrophils from MANC mice express higher levels of S100a8/9, Ngp, and Ly6g compared to other genotypes.
source: Neutrophils from MANC mice express higher levels of neutrophil signature genes, including S100a8/9, Ngp, and Ly6g (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: MANC neutrophils express higher levels of genes associated with pathogen clearance and host tissue damage, including Nos2, Cybb, and Mmp9.
source: These neutrophils also express higher levels of genes associated with pathogen clearance and host tissue damage, including inducible nitric oxide synthase (Nos2), NADPH oxidase (Cybb), and Mmp9.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: MANC neutrophils' glycolytic signature includes higher expression levels of Ldha and Pfkfb3.
source: MANC neutrophils' glycolytic signature includes higher expression levels of Ldha and Pfkfb3.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Neutrophils from MANA, MANB, and B6 mice expressed higher levels of Tlr2, Il1b, and MHC II isoforms (H2-Ab1 and H2-Eb) compared to MANC.
source: In contrast, neutrophils from MANA, MANB, and B6 mice expressed higher levels of specific immune-related genes relevant to defense against Mtb infection including Tlr2, Il1b, and MHC II isoforms (H2-Ab1 and H2-Eb) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The chemokines Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl5, and Ccl6 were highly differentially expressed between the mouse lines.
source: Other genes that were highly differentially expressed between the lines were the chemokines Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl5, and Ccl6 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Neutrophils from all lines expressed very low levels of immunosuppressive proteins and cytokines, with the exception of IL-1R antagonist (Il1rn).
source: Neutrophils from all lines expressed very low levels of immunosuppressive proteins and cytokines, with the exception of IL-1R antagonist (Il1rn), which was highly expressed by a subset of MANB neutrophils (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The MANC transcriptional signature is unique to neutrophils from this line and not a common feature of high bacterial burden or neutrophil-driven pathology during Mtb infection.
source: We compared this signature with the transcriptional signature of Sp140–/– and again found that the MANC transcriptional signature is unique to neutrophils from this line and not a common feature of high bacterial burden or neutrophil-driven pathology during Mtb infection (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of gene expression data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Neutrophils from the lungs of Mtb-infected MANC mice were uniquely found to exhibit an immature transcriptional phenotype dominated by G3 and G4 cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that neutrophils from the lungs of Mtb-infected MANC mice were uniquely found to exhibit an immature transcriptional phenotype dominated by G3 (immature neutrophils) and G4 (mature neutrophils prior to release from bone marrow).
evidence: This claim is supported by neutrophil staging analysis data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: All other genotypes were dominated by mature peripheral neutrophils G5a, G5b, and G5c cells.
source: All other genotypes were dominated by mature peripheral neutrophils G5a, G5b, and G5c cells, as expected (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by neutrophil staging analysis data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: All genotypes possessed naïve CD4 T cells, Th1 differentiated T cells, Ki67+ proliferating T cells, and cytotoxic T cells expressing granzyme B and perforin.
source: All genotypes possessed naïve CD4 T cells, Th1 differentiated T cells, Ki67+ proliferating T cells, and cytotoxic T cells expressing granzyme B and perforin (cytotoxic CD4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq analysis of CD4 T cells presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: B6 mice uniquely had a population of terminally differentiated Th1 T cells that express KLRG1 and high levels of IFN-γ.
source: B6 mice uniquely had a population of what appear to be terminally differentiated Th1 T cells that express KLRG1 and high levels of IFN-γ (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq analysis of CD4 T cells presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: KLRG1+ IFN-γ high T cells have been previously identified as a non-protective T cell subset in B6 mice.
source: These cells have been previously identified as a non-protective T cell subset in B6 mice (Sakai et al., 2014; Cyktor et al., 2013; Lindenstrøm et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: None of the Manaus lines appear to have the KLRG1+ IFN-γ high T cell subset, even in the susceptible MANC line.
source: It is interesting that none of the Manaus lines appear to have this subset of T cells, even in the susceptible MANC line.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq analysis of CD4 T cells presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Markers of T cell activation and differentiation, including Cd44, Pdcd1, Tigit, and Cd69, were not substantially different across mouse lines.
source: Other markers of T cell activation and differentiation, including Cd44, Pdcd1, Tigit, and Cd69, were not substantially different across mouse lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that major phenotypic differences in CD4 T cells themselves, separate from their propensity for trafficking into or surviving within the granuloma, do not underlie the susceptibility of MANC mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq analysis of CD4 T cells presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Major phenotypic differences in CD4 T cells themselves do not underlie the susceptibility of MANC mice.
source: Other markers of T cell activation and differentiation, including Cd44, Pdcd1, Tigit, and Cd69, were not substantially different across mouse lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that major phenotypic differences in CD4 T cells themselves, separate from their propensity for trafficking into or surviving within the granuloma, do not underlie the susceptibility of MANC mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of differences in T cell activation markers across genotypes.

claim: CD11b+/Ly6g− macrophage/monocyte-like cells fell into 14 distinct clusters based on scRNAseq analysis.
source: CD11b+/Ly6g− macrophage/monocyte-like cells were also mapped using our scRNAseq data and were found to fall into 14 distinct clusters, many but not all of which were genotype specific (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq clustering analysis presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Alveolar macrophages were observed in every genotype of mouse.
source: As expected, alveolar macrophages were observed in every genotype of mouse (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq analysis presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: B6 and MANA were dominated by monocytes whereas MANB and MANC mice had clear macrophage populations.
source: No clear pattern in terms of distribution of cell types emerged from analysis of markers for macrophages (Adgre1), monocytes (Cx3cr1), and inflammatory monocytes (Ly6c) (Figure 6A), although B6 and MANA were dominated by monocytes whereas MANB and MANC mice had clear macrophage populations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq analysis presented in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Monocyte/macrophages from MANC mice had a higher propensity to express Nos2.
source: Similar to what we previously observed in neutrophils, monocyte/macrophages from MANC mice had a higher propensity to express Nos2 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: No genes indicative of macrophage function, including IL1b, Arg1, Tnf, and Cybb, were differentially expressed across genotypes.
source: No other genes indicative of macrophage function, including IL1b, Arg1, Tnf, and Cybb, were differentially expressed across genotypes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: MANC macrophages exhibited very high levels of expression of S100a9 and S100a8.
source: Interestingly, MANC macrophages also exhibited very high levels of expression of S100a9 and S100a8, genes more typically associated with neutrophil function (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Expression of S100a8, S100a9, Ngp, and lcn2 was dramatically increased in MANC mice across multiple cell types.
source: Interestingly, we found that expression of a small number of genes was dramatically increased in MANC mice, and that this signature was dominated by genes that are often thought to be relatively neutrophil specific, including Ngp (neutrophil granule protein), S100a9, S100a8, and lcn2 (lipocalin 2) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Higher expression of neutrophil-specific genes in MANC was not solely driven by higher expression levels in neutrophils, as increased expression was observed across all cell types analyzed.
source: Higher expression of these genes was not solely driven by higher expression levels in neutrophils, as we observed increased expression of these genes across all cell types analyzed, which included major immune cell populations as well as epithelial cells and fibroblasts isolated from lungs (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Expression of Ngp was observed at highest levels in neutrophils in the ImmGen database, with dramatically lower levels of expression across other immune cell types.
source: As expected, we found that expression of Ngp was observed at highest levels in neutrophils, with dramatically lower levels of expression across other immune cell types (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of ImmGen database data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Expression of neutrophil-specific genes across many cell types appears to be a unique feature of MANC mice.
source: Thus, expression of these neutrophil-specific genes across many cell types appears to be a unique feature of MANC mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of widespread expression of neutrophil genes in MANC and comparison with ImmGen data.

claim: Wild mice exhibited a range in susceptibility at an early time point after Mtb infection.
source: Here we used a new collection of inbred wild mice to study the outcome of infection with Mtb. Wild mice exhibited a range in susceptibility at an early time point after infection as well as diversity in the immune responses to infection (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by CFU and immune response data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Neutrophils are thought to be an important driver of susceptibility to TB in both mice and humans.
source: Neutrophils are thought to be an important driver of susceptibility to the outcome of TB in both mice and humans (Mishra et al., 2017; Berry et al., 2010; Nandi and Behar, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: It has been proposed that neutrophils are detrimental to Mtb infection due to generation of lung inflammation and NETosis.
source: It has been proposed that the neutrophils are detrimental to infection due to generation of lung inflammation and NETosis (Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Neutrophils are highly abundant in the lungs of infected MANC mice.
source: We found that neutrophils are highly abundant in the lungs of infected MANC mice, and that neutrophils drive the susceptibility of this line (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figures 4A-E.

claim: Neutrophils drive the susceptibility of MANC mice to Mtb infection.
source: We found that neutrophils are highly abundant in the lungs of infected MANC mice, and that neutrophils drive the susceptibility of this line (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by neutrophil depletion experiments presented in Figures 4D-E.

claim: Neutrophils in MANB mice are more discrete and dispersed throughout the tissue compared to MANC.
source: Histological data from the lungs of MANC mice show Ly6G staining for neutrophils reveals large aggregates of staining within the lesions of MANC mice, whereas neutrophils in MANB mice are more discrete and dispersed throughout the tissue (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data presented in Figure 4G-H.

claim: Neutrophil clusters from MANC mice have high expression of genes that contribute to neutrophil degranulation as well as superoxide and NO production.
source: scRNAseq expression analysis shows that neutrophil clusters from MANC mice have a high expression of genes that contribute to neutrophil degranulation as well as superoxide and NO production, indicating potential for tissue destruction during infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression analysis presented in Figures 4M and 5A.

claim: Neutrophils from MANC mice exhibit a more activated glycolytic transcriptional signature when compared with B6 or other MAN lines.
source: In addition, neutrophils from these mice exhibit a more activated glycolytic transcriptional signature when compared with B6 or other MAN lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression analysis showing enrichment for glycolysis genes.

claim: The transcriptional phenotype of protected MANB is strikingly different from MANC, with an expression profile associated with protective genes, including Tlr2 and Il1b.
source: The transcriptional phenotype of protected MANB is strikingly different from MANC, with an expression profile that is associated with protective genes, including Tlr2 and Il1b.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression analysis presented in Figure 5A.

claim: MANB neutrophils may not drive pathology during Mtb infection due to expression of protective factors combined with a less activated phenotype.
source: We hypothesize that expression of these protective factors combined with a less activated phenotype means that MANB neutrophils may not drive pathology during Mtb infection.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed gene expression differences between MANB and MANC neutrophils.

claim: Neutrophils from highly susceptible MANC mice expressed high levels of S100a8 and S100a9 relative to other mouse lines, including the highly susceptible Sp140–/– line.
source: We found that neutrophils from highly susceptible MANC mice expressed high levels of S100a8 and S100a9 relative to other mouse lines, including the highly susceptible Sp140–/– line.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression analysis presented in Figure 5A-B.

claim: S100a8/a9 expression has been associated with numerous inflammatory states, including severe COVID-19.
source: S100a8/a9 expression has been associated with numerous inflammatory states, including severe COVID-19 (Udeh et al., 2021; Silvin et al., 2020; Boucher et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Depletion of S100a8 and S100a9 was shown to improve chronic control of Mtb infection in mice.
source: In addition, depletion of S100a8 and S100a9 was shown to improve chronic control of Mtb infection in mice (Scott et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Expression of S100a8/a9 has been associated with progression of humans to active TB disease.
source: Finally, expression of these genes has been associated with progression of humans to active disease (Scott et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: MANC mice may represent an attractive model for studying the role of S100A8/A9 in TB as well as other inflammatory diseases.
source: Thus, MANC mice may represent an attractive model for studying the role of S100A8/A9 in TB as well as other inflammatory diseases.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential utility of MANC mice based on their S100a8/a9 expression.

claim: IFN-γ is mainly produced by CD4 T cells early during Mtb infection.
source: Another intriguing aspect of the immune response to Mtb is the role of IFN-γ during infection. IFN-γ is mainly produced by CD4 T cells early during infection, and a lack of IFN-γ results in extreme susceptibility, with mice succumbing to infection (Green et al., 2013; Flynn et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A lack of IFN-γ results in extreme susceptibility to Mtb, with mice succumbing to infection.
source: Another intriguing aspect of the immune response to Mtb is the role of IFN-γ during infection. IFN-γ is mainly produced by CD4 T cells early during infection, and a lack of IFN-γ results in extreme susceptibility, with mice succumbing to infection (Green et al., 2013; Flynn et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IFN-γ is required for prevention of bacterial dissemination to other tissues during Mtb infection.
source: Furthermore, IFN-γ is required for prevention of bacterial dissemination to other tissues (Sakai et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Increased IFN-γ responses in the lung do not seem to correlate with resistance to Mtb infection or improved responses to vaccination and can lead to exacerbated disease.
source: However, increased IFN-γ responses in the lung do not seem to correlate with resistance to infection or improved responses to vaccination and can lead to exacerbated disease (Tameris et al., 2013; Sakai et al., 2016; Leal et al., 2001; Majlessi et al., 2006; Mittrücker et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: T cell-mediated IFN-γ independent mechanisms contribute to control of Mtb infection, including through GM-CSF production by CD4 T cells.
source: While local IFN-γ production might be necessary for full control of infection in B6 mice, additional research has shown effects of T cell-mediated IFN-γ independent mechanisms that contribute to control of infection, including through GM-CSF production by CD4 T cells (Rothchild et al., 2014; Rothchild et al., 2017; Van Dis et al., 2022) and the production of IL-17 (Gallegos et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Production of IL-17 contributes to control of Mtb infection.
source: While local IFN-γ production might be necessary for full control of infection in B6 mice, additional research has shown effects of T cell-mediated IFN-γ independent mechanisms that contribute to control of infection, including through GM-CSF production by CD4 T cells (Rothchild et al., 2014; Rothchild et al., 2017; Van Dis et al., 2022) and the production of IL-17 (Gallegos et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Several mouse lines in the cohort showed restriction of bacterial growth in the first weeks post-infection equally well but with widely differing IFN-γ+ T cell profiles.
source: Several mouse lines in the cohort showed restriction of bacterial growth in the first weeks post-infection equally well but with widely differing IFN-γ+ T cell profiles.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 1 and 2 showing variability in IFN-γ responses despite similar CFU control.

claim: SARA mice exhibited enhanced control of bacterial burden but very low numbers of IFN-γ+ T cells compared to B6 mice.
source: SARA mice exhibited enhanced control of bacterial burden (Figure 1D), but very low numbers of IFN-γ+ T cells compared to B6 mice (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 1D, 2K, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Control of infection in SARA mice suggests either optimal localization of IFN-γ producing T cells to bacterial-containing lesions or the presence of IFN-γ or T cell-independent control of infection.
source: This suggests either optimal localization of the few IFN-γ producing T cells to the bacterial-containing lesions, thereby allowing for highly efficient induction of local IFN-γ driven protective responses in the lesions, or the presence of IFN-γ or T cell-independent control of infection.
evidence: This is a speculation about possible mechanisms underlying the SARA phenotype.

claim: Homing of Mtb-specific T cells to the lung parenchyma is essential for interaction with activated macrophages to induce control of infection.
source: It has previously been shown that homing of Mtb-specific T cells to the lung parenchyma is essential for interaction with activated macrophages to induce control of infection; however, signals that allow for T cell penetration into granulomas have not been fully elicited (Sakai et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A correlation was found between higher B cell numbers and improved resistance to Mtb infection.
source: For example, we found a correlation between higher B cell numbers and improved resistance to infection; whether B cells may play a role in infection control is a question that can be examined using these lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis data presented in Figure 2I.
